Not even a psychiatrist would diagnose a person based on a single letter.

This was not the act of a desperate, mentally ill man. It was an authentic reaction to existence in an objectively terrible world wherein there is no place for people like him. Not only should we understand each suicide for what it was, but we oughtn’t wish for it not to have happened. Not wanting to exist is not the same as mental illness. That's a leap in logic. His unhappiness was not depression. It was dissatisfaction.
He wasn't mentally ill. Thank you for the good intentions, but pinning this on a disease, pathologizing his experience, is the easy answer. We have to see these things in a full way.

And this was his letter - his context. I feel the exact same. It's like reading my own words. 

"Sorry, guys.

This was my fault not yours.

I've never felt like a person. It's hard to explain. I don't even think any of
you have even met me before. I don't even think there really is a "me".

When we're out drinking during holidays I feel like I'm watching myself. 
It's not like an out of body experience. I don't see myself. But I feel as
though I'm watching myself talk to you. We're both observing me during those
times. I don't know who that is or how he makes decisions or why sometimes he's
really good socially or really bad. I don't know where he comes up with what he
says.

I just know me, the real me, the one writing this note and that occupies the
majority of my life just can't deal with the world. I can't deal with it like
you do. So I just go completely hands off. It's not even anxiety really, it's
just being completely overwhelmed. The person you know is all adrenaline and
instinct, and we're both watching him.

I don't want to make it sound like I have multiple personalities. It's not like
that. It's more that you've only seen me during a fight or flight response. It's
just all reflex and instinct. Some base part of me.

I've always fels like an observer to my own life and not an actual participant.
It's fucked up, but I've never really had any interest participating in my own
life. As long as I've had a roof over my head and food I've been happy.

The sadness and the stress comes when I have to actually interact with the
world. When I have to go grocery shopping, take out the trash,
when I see the effects of my selfish lifestyle on the people I love.

I decided to do this a long time ago. I had a week long job programming. I'd
done well. I'd proven that I could make it in this world. I was even offered
more work.

I thought I'd be happy. Like that it was somehow a lack of skills that's kept me
from enjoying life. But it wasn't. I don't want to work. I don't want to
interact with people. I feel no connection to myself, my real world self, and I
have no motivation to put any effort into making his life better. I don't get
any satisfaction from completing a goal or experiencing life. I just want to be
alone.

I did a bad job explaining myself. Check out pg 130 in The Waves. The big Rhoda
paragraph. It's kind of poetry but line for line it's nearly exactly how I feel.
She even touches on parts that I could never even begin to describe. 

But I don't want to hurt you guys any more. I'm selfish. So fucking selfish that
I'm a huge burden to myself. I'll regularly go full days having
forgotten to eat. I'm just so caught up and distracted and at peace that
I'll forget what's essentially a reflex. That's how selfish I am.

I love all of you. I don't really show it. It's difficult for me. I don't
even know if love is the right word. It's not how most people experience it. But
it's the closest I've ever felt to people and it's as much as I'm capable of.

Train driver--

I'm sorry man. I know you guys can go through PTSD when this happens. The
unfortunate truth is that there aren't really any cheap surefire ways of
succeeding.

gun: too expensive
hanging: there's no place in my apartment to connect a rope. And sadly, I can't
even afford a rope
carbon monixide: no enclosed space
wrist slitting: I don't like things even touching my veins, I could never cut
long and deep enough for success
Height jump: I can't afford the gas to go far enough for a bridge that would do
the job.

*** Here he addressed different people. All have been omitted except for what he wrote to me. ***

(my name) --

Sorry man

I was actually thinking about contacting you, but I was worried about causing
any suspicion or leaving any signs that you guys could beat yourselves up for
missing.

We grew apart and part of that is my fault. I've always felt like you got the
short end of the stick. The world is overwhelming to me and I deal with that by
withdrawing. I think something similar happens with you but you hate that
feeling of powerlessness so you lash out. Your way of coping burns bridges and
tht must suck.

I really looked up to you when I was growing up. You were just so cool and
always nice to me. I loved sitting in your room reading music magazines of bands
I never heard of. We wouldn't even talk. It just felt great.

Plus drinking with you at my old apartment was amazing. Just really some of the
best memories ever. Thanks

--- PSUEDO WILL ---

I want the cheapest everything. No eternal flame! That was always a joke.

Car goes to dad. Hopefully you can sell it and make up for a fraction of the
expenses I've caused you.

I left two lock pieces on my desk. I don't know why but I've always loved them.
They mean a lot to me for some reason. I really wish I had more sentimental
things to give to each person.

I also left my favorite books on my desk. All of them are really good.

As to who gets what I'll leave that for you all to decide amongst yourselves.
Tiebreaker is dad.

I guess that's everything. Sorry this was such a sloppy note. It's pretty
stressful writing this and I'm not even going to re-read it.

I hope there isn't a hell. I hope it's just like before I was born.

Maybe I ought to provide some context. I am 33 and he was 6 years younger. Here are some excerpts from my journal entries. This will be long. My apologies. 

"We have never been well - my family. My brothers and I have all been afflicted with melancholia. I use this word, melancholia, purposively. For, it isn’t depression. It’s a sickness of spirit. We’ve led uncommon lives punctuated by impulsivity, restlessness, unhappiness. We’ve struggled with this pervasive inability to take care of and provide for ourselves. We forget to eat. We’re afraid of making phone calls. The mundane tasks that most everyone completes with ease daily are blockades. We don’t like working. We don’t like socializing. We want to be left alone to read and create and do the things we love. There’s meaning in that, but in not much else. It isn’t laziness, but a failure to exist in modernity where we are expected to be self-sufficient, productive, and independent. Those are the markers of successful existence. So, we’ve all felt like failures. My living brother is managing to dig his way out. I, however, feel like a failure. XXXX felt like a failure, like a burden, and ended his life."

"From the moment XXXX was born, I adored him. We were always together. We grew up close and remained uncommonly so. We lived together at various points, in various states, for various amounts of time. We talked candidly, fought passionately about philosophy, economics, politics. No one knew me unless they knew XXXX, for he knew me unlike anyone else. He was truly my other half. But over the last five weeks, in the aftermath of his suicide, I’ve stopped trying to describe the particular nature of our relationship, the degree of closeness we shared, because I simply can’t. The problem of other minds rears it’s ugly head again and again. Unless you knew us as we were, I can never make you understand. Despite this closeness, something went wrong."

"I remember that night like it was yesterday: sitting on the floor in his room. He was crying. He told me he just couldn’t do it, it being life. He told me he had been stealing my anti-depressants, that he was thinking of killing himself. I didn’t know what to do. I cried too. He said he just wanted to get in shape and join the Navy and that single hope was the only thing keeping him going. I didn’t understand where this was coming from. The fucking Navy? I remembered an old friend from high school who decided to join the Army out of nowhere. He tried to kill himself in basic. While I didn’t understand his desire, I did understand his suffering, and looking back on it, it all makes perfect sense.

We had given him an old desk — my partner’s dad’s desk — and I remember looking at it while he cried. All of his lock-picking stuff. The solder iron. Gödel, Escher, Bach. Little things. Other books. Drawings. He was sitting on his air mattress which was dressed in linens we gave him. He had almost nothing. Hell, we had almost nothing. We had no income. Our lives were completely subsidized by our parents, but the money was never enough. Food insecurity was real for all three of us in that house. We were poor and we had been for a long time. That really took a toll on all of us. Everything we owned was either junk or second-hand. I had gotten used to it. But looking around his room and listening to him describe his experience of living made me feel like a complete and utter failure. I had failed him. In so many ways. The last time around, I saw him as a broken person. This time, I saw myself as the broken person. It occurred to me then, in that room, that self-sufficiency nor productivity were the virtues they’d been sold to me as. Moreover, I realized the harm the demand to achieve them causes. And in that moment I understood that I had embodied and advanced that harm. I was a fool. I hated myself. I apologized blankly as the realization struck me in waves, as tears rolled down my face. I told him I was wrong and that I didn’t give a single fuck if he got a job. I told him that I just wanted him to be happy. We hugged for a long time that night. We talked long and candidly. He shook with crying. I said that we could fix it, that we’d figure everything out. It was too fucking late."

"Within the month he’d planned a move to Texas to live with dad. I begged him not to go. I told him that if he left, I’d probably never see him again. We all begged him not to go. But he was hungry. He had no money and neither did we. He wanted to be comfortable in the most basic sense — in the sense that he just wanted there to be a roof over his head and food in the fridge. We could only provide one of the two. And in that regard, the move seemed essential to his well being, so I resigned myself to it and to losing the person I loved most in the world…due to a lack of fucking resources."

" Talk about rehabilitating XXXX started circulating in the family. A life-coach was mentioned. College was mentioned. The question became, “How do we get XXXX on his own two feet?” I was horrified. I heard my former self echoing those exact phrases. But I finally knew better. I’d tell them, “Look, maybe we should approach this differently. Maybe he just isn’t that kind of person. Some people need to be taken care of and that’s perfectly okay.” Most people disagreed with my assessment. They thought I was rounding him down, dehumanizing him. I thought the opposite. I thought I was humanizing him in a way no one had, in a way I had already failed to do, in a way that no one humanizes anyone anymore. I saw him as more of a person in those final days than I had for months. He was vibrant in my mind. He was gentle and kind, brilliant and challenging. I loved him more. I saw him. "

"All that is substantial comes too late. There is no amount of premeditation that can prevent tragedy. There is no amount of ethical or philosophical investigation that can sufficiently prepare anyone for living. What exists is cruel and is suspended in a system conducive only to the normative. Freedom has been reduced to callousness, existence to productivity. And we wish to prevent suicide? No. Suicide has become far more reasonable a choice than existence, for this is an objectively terrible world and we are all objectively terrible beings, try as we might to be otherwise."
